title: Lifting plans for Athletes (programming for sports)
summary: NH explains how athletes should fit hypertrophy training around their sport: play the sport first, sport-specific drills second, and weights last at about 10% of time and energy. He gives minimalist twice-weekly 'twin templates' in the description (Purist for athletes, Hybrid for size plus function) for cycling, swimming and racket sports, with reps in reserve, no failure, and no heavy sessions the day before practice.
claims: Strength sports (powerlifting, strongman) are excluded because they already use barbells; adding hypertrophy work would pull them away from what matters, while sports like track pair well with lifting
He says bodybuilding and powerlifting are like cousins who shouldn't mix, while lifting and an unrelated sport combine well
An athlete is someone who puts function before form; anyone else is a hobbyist
He trained for football for two years and basketball for three, but he is a pure bodybuilder, so his athlete programs lean towards size
Programs come in two versions: Purist for people who only care about function, Hybrid for people who want size and function
Athletes' lifting programs should be minimalist because they already put maximum effort into their sport
The order of priority is playing the sport, then sport-specific drills that copy its movements, then hypertrophy training
Copying sport movements with weights, like throwing uppercuts holding dumbbells, does not build sport-specific power; boxers who do it are training their cardio
Every top pro athlete does resistance training at some point; muscle multiplies power output, but only if it is the right muscle for the sport
Muscle that doesn't fit the sport can hurt performance; a sprinter with huge pecs is slowed by the extra mass and oxygen demand
Split time and energy roughly 70% playing the sport, 20% drills and 10% hypertrophy; advanced athletes might go 60/20/20
Lifting causes more muscle damage than sport for the same time; 40 minutes of team practice might equal about 15 minutes of top-set lifting in recovery cost
Keep the technical difficulty of lifts low for athletes: no Olympic cleans or advanced ring work, because the sport already demands all their skill-learning time
Athletes don't need extra cardio-heavy lifting; their sport already covers conditioning, so lifting should target muscle fibre damage the sport leaves untouched
Never do a heavy lifting session the day before practice or competition
Athletes should stimulate, not annihilate: train at around 70-80% of capacity with reps in reserve and never to failure; going all-out belongs in competition
Short, intense, low-rep top sets spread through the week reduce injury risk and leave room for the sport
Diet must also serve the sport: athletes should not bulk for a bigger bench or cut for a six-pack
Doing two similar pursuits at once usually means you are mediocre at both; you must make one the priority
You lift to get better at your sport; the day you lift just to lift, you stop being an athlete
Every template is meant for twice a week (Day A, Day B); 3-4 times a week risks athletic performance and recovery. Purists can add the optional conditioning Day C, Hybrids should repeat Day A instead

Cycling Purist template: Day A squats 3x3, hyperextensions 3x10-12 plus seated calf raises 3x12-15, push-ups plus straight-arm planks AMRAP; Day B RDLs 3x6-8, lunges 3x10-12 plus triceps extensions 3x12-15, forearm planks plus single-leg hip thrusts AMRAP
Cycling Day C conditioning: 3x500 m dashes plus single-leg calf raises AMRAP, shiko 5x10-25 plus bicycle crunches AMRAP

Swimming/water polo Purist template: Day A barbell rows 3x8-10, OHP 3x6-10 plus wide-grip pulldowns 3x12-15, rear lateral raises 3x10-15 plus flutter kicks; Day B weighted pull-ups 3x5, DB rows 3x8-12 plus DB flies 3x10-15, lateral raises plus lying leg raises
Hybrid templates add arm, neck, trap and leg isolation work (curls, hammer curls, neck curls, shrugs, skull crushers, Bulgarian split squats) to the Purist base
Racket sports template uses Swiss-bar or neutral-grip DB bench 3x6-10, reverse lunges 3x12-15, finger curls 3x6-10, and trap-bar or Jefferson deadlifts 1-3x5
exercises: low back-friendly hinge for racket sports
sumo leg conditioning on Day C
too technical; takes skill time away from the sport
